Chapter 1: Growing Up in a World Shaped by Injustice
Childhood memories have a way of carrying the weight of the world, don’t they? Even when you’re a kid, and the world feels way too big to ever make sense.
Imagine growing up in a neighborhood where helicopters buzz overhead, and police cars drive by as often as the ice cream truck you wait for all summer. That’s where our story begins—a place in Los Angeles where a young girl realized pretty early on that feeling safe was something other people just seemed to expect.
The streets were full of laughter and games, but underneath it all, there was this hum of worry. You never really shook the feeling that someone close might not make it home, or that the world outside your door could turn dangerous in an instant.
Through all that uncertainty, family was everything. Her mom, working nonstop—sometimes two or three jobs—was like a superhero. She did whatever it took to keep food on the table and the lights shining. She fought hard to shield her kids from the toughest blows of poverty and discrimination.
Her dad wasn’t always around, but even his absence had a way of shaping things—making the family stronger in some ways, and leaving questions in others. Siblings became your teammates and secret-keepers, helping each other get through school, friendships, and all those unspoken rules about how to just get by.
In this world, right and wrong didn’t always look the way you’d expect. Schools were packed, resources stretched thin, and it sometimes felt like teachers looked right through you. Instead of nurturing curiosity, the focus was on keeping order.
And the police? They were everywhere. But their presence wasn’t exactly reassuring. You learned quickly that when they showed up, it usually meant trouble, not help.
It didn’t take long—even as a kid—to notice that life wasn’t fair for everyone. Some families seemed to float through their days, never weighed down by the stresses that others carried. No one explained why, but you could feel it in every part of your life—in how neighbors treated each other, how authority figures talked to you, and in the way the world seemed to value some lives over others.
Still, even with all these challenges, there was joy. Family cookouts, music, and laughter brought moments of relief. The community—though worn down by poverty and neglect—always found ways to celebrate. People looked out for each other, shared what little they had, and offered comfort when things got tough. Those everyday moments of connection? They were everything—a reminder that love and resilience could take root, even in the harshest conditions.
As the years went by, it became impossible to ignore the realities of systemic racism. Friends and family members got caught up in the criminal justice system—sometimes for things that seemed so small, but carried huge consequences. The fear of losing someone, whether to violence or incarceration, was always there. It shaped every decision, every dream.
And yet, despite it all, hope survived. There was always this quiet belief that things could get better—that justice was something you could reach for, even if it sometimes felt just out of grasp.
